2. The petitioner filed an application on 31-12-2001 before the Court of learned Magistrate, 1st Class, Sadar Chittagong under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the opposite-parties stating that the petitioner is the owner and possessor of the case land and he has constructed a tin-shed house where he is dealing grocery business in the name and style as "Ekata Trading". The opposite-parties have no right, title, interest and possession over the land and structure therein. The opposite-party intended to take rent of the said shop but having failed he is trying to dispossess the petitioner from the rightful ownership and possession. The petitioner tried to resist them and there arises serious breach of peace including committing of murder. Therefore, a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure may be started. 

 3. The learned Magistrate directed the Officer-in-Charge of Mirsarai PS to maintain peace and status quo in the case land and to report. On receipt of the said report the learned Magistrate converted the case from section 144 to 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and directed the opposite-parties to submit written statement and the learned Magistrate transferred the case to the Court of another Magistrate presided over by Mr Md Moniruzzaman Khan for trial and disposal. 

 13. It appears that on an application filed by the 1st party the learned Magistrate initiated proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 31-12-2001 and on receipt of the report from the police on 15-2-2002 converted the said proceeding into section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and transferred the case to the Court of Mr Md Muniruzzaman Khan, another Magistrate for trial. The 1st party petitioner filed an application for appointment of receiver. The learned Magistrate being satisfied passed an order under the proviso of section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and appointed Officer-in-Charge of Mirsarai PS as receiver on 27-8-2002. Being aggrieved, the 2nd party preferred Criminal Revision under sections 435/439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. After hearing the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 6th Court, Chittagong allowed the criminal revision and set aside the order of appointment of receiver dated 27-8-2002. The learned Magistrate, Chittagong directed the Officer- in-Charge, Mirsarai to hand over the possession of the shop to the 2nd party. Against the said order the 1st party petitioner preferred Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 118 of 2003 before this Hon'ble Court and obtained Rule and an order of stay operation of the said impugned order but in the meantime the 2nd party obtained possession from the receiver according to the order passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge. The petitioner filed an application to the learned Magistrate for appointment of receiver along with order passed by , the High Court Division. In the meantime the 2nd party filed an application under section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, to stay all further proceedings of the said proceeding. The learned Magistrate after hearing both the parties appointed Officer-in-Charge of Mirsarai PS as receiver and rejected the application for stay of all further proceeding of the said 145 proceeding filed by the 2nd party under section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Against the said order the 2nd party preferred another criminal revision before the learned Sessions Judge under sections 435/439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and after hearing the learned Advocates of the parties the learned Sessions Judge set aside the order dated 15-4-2003 passed by the learned Additional Magistrate and stayed all further proceedings of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 206 of 2001. The 1st party petitioner again preferred miscellaneous application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained Rule and stay operation of the said judgment passed by the learned Sessions Judge and also obtained a direction to continue the trial as usual. It appears that the proceeding was initiated on 31-12-2001 and during the pendency of the said proceeding the 2nd party dispossessed the petitioner on 28-1-2002 but from the report 2002 the learned Advocate for the 2nd party submits that the action of dispossession has already been made on 28-1-2002 and there is no apprehension of breach of peace but from the report of the police dated 15-2-2002 it appears that there was serious apprehension of breach of peace. Accordingly, the learned Magistrate converted the proceeding of section 144 to 145 proceeding. The dispossession during the pendency of the proceeding is not a valid possession in the eye of law. In the instant case the learned Additional Sessions Judge directed the receiver to hand over possession to the 2nd party without having any evidence and such direction cannot be supported by any Court of law. The learned Magistrate passed the order according to second proviso of sub-section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It has been held in the case of Saber Ahmed and 30 others vs Amir Hamja and 6 others reported in 31 DLR 169 in a full Bench decision comprising Mr Justice Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Mr Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud and Mr Justice Aminul Islam Chowdhury where it has been held that order of attachment can be passed at any moment when the case is pending before the Magistrate if the Magistrate is satisfied that emergency of the situation demands that It is not necessary that notice must be served on the parties to appear and submit statement. In the said case Mr Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud held a different view that the Magistrate not empowered to pass an order of attachment under the 2nd proviso without compliance with the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure i.e. before serving copy of the order on the parties concerned which has followed the case of Osman Gani vs Besharuddin Ahmed reported in 32 DLR 53 but such decision has not been supported by majority view and the majority view was that the 2nd proviso of sub-section (4) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a proviso of entire section itself because the expression "pending his decision under this section" has been issued. In other words, when the entire dispute awaits determination under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure then in the case of emergency. "If the Magistrate considers the case one of emergency" he may at any time attach the subject of dispute pending his decision "under this section" and that a Magistrate is fully empowered by law to pass an order under the 2nd proviso of sub-section (4) by way of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure attaching the property if he considers that it is a case of emergency, immediately drawing up proceeding under sub-section (1) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It has been held in the case of Md Shamsul Alam vs Kiron Chandra Shome and another reported in 31 DLR (AD) 150 which has also considered the case of full Bench Saber Ahmed and 30 others vs Amir Hamja and 6 others reported in 31 DLR 169 where it has been held that the Court has inherent jurisdiction to pass any interlocutory order in exercise of its jurisdiction. In case of emergency, power has been conferred upon Magistrate to initiate proceeding on the disputed property and appointment of receiver are drawn up proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure if the Magistrate is satisfied that there is likelihood of breach of peace regarding any immovable property. The learned Additional Sessions Judge directed the receiver to hand over possession to the 2nd party without any evidence and without discussing and determining as to who was in possession before initiation of the proceeding and, as such, the direction is not a proper order in accordance with law. When there was serious apprehension of immediate breach of peace and in case of emergency the learned Magistrate was satisfied and drawn up proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on the basis of report of the police on 15-2-2002 and, as such, serious apprehension of breach of peace still in existence as it appears from the application of both the parties where an order of attachment and appointment of receiver was legally made under 2nd proviso of section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent serious apprehension of immediate breach of peace and the Special Bench by majority view ruled that Magistrate is fully empowered by law to pass an order under the 2nd proviso of sub-section 4 attaching the property if he considers that it is a case of emergency immediately after drawing up proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Such majority view was upheld by the Appellate Division. The question arises before us now that whether this Court in exercise of power of jurisdiction of 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure can set aside the impugned order dated 23-11-2002 and the order dated 29-4-2003 which are held to be illegal on the face of it. In view of the decision of the full Bench reported in 31 DLR 169, it has been held in the case of Rita Kundu vs Akbar Ali and others reported in 1986 BLD 185 to the effect that under section 561 A nothing shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of the High Court Division to make such order as may be necessarily to give effect to any order made under this Court or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 561A should not be invoked where some other remedy is available. Section 561A is not alternative jurisdiction nor an additional jurisdiction but its jurisdiction is preserved in the interest of justice to redress the grievance of any party where there is no other remedy available. In the instant case and the facts and circumstances of the case we observe an illegality has been committed to make the impugned order and the petitioner has no other remedy under the law. The initial remedy available to the party to check redress before the learned Magistrate and accordingly, 1st party availed and filed an application and in the case of emergency and immediate apprehension breach of peace the petitioner is entitled to an order under 2nd proviso of sub-section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he got such an order and Magistrate on satisfaction attached the property under 2nd proviso of section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which cannot be said that the order is not a proper order. But we find that such order was passed not in accordance with law rather, we hold the direction to the receiver to hand over possession to the 2nd party without any evidence is not sustainable in law. Once a proceeding began with preliminary order, it must be ended by following inquiry and with final order. Admittedly, the 2nd party dispossessed the petitioner on 28-1-2002 while the case land was under proceeding and on the said dispossession the police reported immediate serious apprehension of breach of peace on 15-2-2002 and consequently, the learned Magistrate passed an order under the 2nd proviso of sub-section 4 of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It has been held in the case of Rita Kundu vs Akbar Ali reported in 1986 BLD 185 that when an order of attachment and appointment of receiver was legally made by the Magistrate to prevent serious apprehension of immediate breach of peace, such order is to be restored by setting aside the order of Sessions Judge who illegally set aside the order of the Magistrate in exercise of inherent jurisdiction of High Court Division for securing ends of justice. Both the orders passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge illegally interrupted and diverted the ordinary course of Code of Criminal Procedure which cannot be supported by this Court. The learned Additional Sessions Judge erroneously stayed all further proceeding of the said criminal proceeding which cannot be appreciated. At the time of issuance of Rule this Court directed the learned Magistrate to proceed with the proceeding as usual, which is still pending.
